newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Final draft of Brazil telcom bill sent to panel.
newsitem.headline: Final draft of Brazil telcom bill sent to panel.

text.p: A final draft of Brazil's new telecommunications law, which will set down rules for privatization of the sector, was presented to a committee in the lower house of Congress Tuesday, officials said.
Members of the committee asked for two sessions to study the new-look bill, meaning any vote is likely to take place next week at the earliest, they said.
"If everything goes according to plan, then we'll vote next Tuesday," said Deputy Alberto Goldman who is in charge of the legislation in the Chamber of Deputies panel.

Congress approved a constitutional amendment ending the Brazilian state's telecommunications monopoly in 1995. Goldman's bill will provide the legal framework for the government to privatize the federal Telebras system.
The bill does not set down any restrictions on foreign capital taking part in the privatization of Telebras nor in the operating of telecommunications services.
Instead, the bill would give the Brazilian president powers to limit the involvement of foreign capital on a case-by-case basis, depending on Brazil's trade relations with each country in question.
Goldman told reporters Monday that the idea was to give Brazil "bargaining power" in its attempts to remove trade barriers to its exports.

Other important points of the bill include the creation of a National Telecommunications Agency, a new sector regulator which would receive all funds raised from the sale of concession fees to private operators.
The fees, which are expected to run into billions of dollars, would ensure the regulator was an independent body, Goldman said.

Once those costs were covered, the remainder of the concession fees would be funneled into a so-called Universalization Fund, which would seek to widen public access to telecommunications, and then to the National Treasury.
Goldman also said the agency would be given powers to undo what it considers to be a concentration of ownership in the telecommunications sector.
Another article of the law would make the agency the only body responsible for overseeing the sector, ruling out the possibility of third-party contractors being hired to carry out specific tasks.
